name: Low Back Pain
prevalence: About 8 in 10 U.S. adults at some point in life
overview: Low back pain is one of the most common reasons people see a doctor — most adults will deal with it at some point. It usually comes from strained muscles, ligaments, or normal wear in the spine, not from anything dangerous. The good news: most episodes get better within a few weeks with gentle movement, over-the-counter pain relievers, and time. Staying active actually helps you heal faster than bed rest.
symptoms: Aching or stiffness in the lower back
Muscle spasms or tightness
Pain that worsens with bending or lifting
Pain that sometimes shoots down a leg (sciatica)
Trouble standing up straight

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: First choice for easing pain and inflammation.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: An option when NSAIDs aren't a good fit.

drugs.name: Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril)
drugs.note: Short-term help for painful muscle spasms.

drugs.name: Physical therapy
drugs.note: Builds strength and helps prevent repeat episodes.

redFlags: Back pain with new loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the groin, or leg weakness can signal serious nerve compression — go to the ER.

name: Neck Pain
prevalence: About 1 in 3 U.S. adults each year
overview: Neck pain is extremely common and usually comes from muscle strain — think long hours at a desk, sleeping in an awkward position, or stress that tightens the shoulders. Most cases ease up within days to a few weeks with gentle stretching, heat, and over-the-counter pain relievers. Less often, a pinched nerve causes pain that travels down the arm; that usually improves too, but takes longer.
symptoms: Stiff, sore neck that's hard to turn
Muscle tightness or spasms
Headaches that start at the base of the skull
Pain that worsens after sitting or driving
Tingling that travels into the shoulder or arm

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Eases pain and calms inflammation.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: A gentler option for mild pain.

drugs.name: Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril)
drugs.note: Used briefly for muscle spasms.

drugs.name: Physical therapy
drugs.note: Stretching and strengthening for lasting relief.

redFlags: Neck pain after a car crash or fall, or pain with fever and a stiff neck, or new arm weakness or numbness, needs emergency care — go to the ER.

name: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
overview: Carpal tunnel syndrome happens when the median nerve gets squeezed as it passes through a narrow tunnel in your wrist, causing numbness, tingling, and weakness in the hand — often worse at night. Typing, assembly work, and conditions like diabetes or pregnancy can raise the risk. Caught early, it often improves with a simple wrist splint; when it doesn't, a brief outpatient surgery brings relief for most people.
symptoms: Numbness or tingling in the thumb and first fingers
Symptoms that wake you up at night
Hand weakness or dropping objects
A 'pins and needles' feeling when gripping
Relief from shaking out the hand

drugs.name: Wrist splint
drugs.note: Worn at night to keep the wrist straight.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: May ease pain, though relief is often modest.

drugs.name: Corticosteroid injection
drugs.note: Reduces swelling around the nerve.

drugs.name: Carpal tunnel release
drugs.note: A short outpatient surgery that relieves the pressure.

redFlags: Constant numbness, a weakening grip, or shrinking muscle at the base of the thumb can mean lasting nerve damage — seek same-day care.

name: Plantar Fasciitis
overview: Plantar fasciitis is irritation of the thick band of tissue (the plantar fascia) that runs along the bottom of your foot, causing stabbing heel pain — classically with the first steps in the morning. Runners, people who stand all day, and those carrying extra weight get it most. It's stubborn but rarely serious: stretching, supportive shoes, and time resolve most cases within several months.
symptoms: Stabbing heel pain with the first steps of the day
Pain after (not usually during) exercise
Tenderness at the bottom of the heel
Pain after long periods of standing
Stiffness that eases as you move

drugs.name: Stretching exercises
drugs.note: Daily calf and foot stretches are the core treatment.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Takes the edge off heel pain.

drugs.name: Orthotic shoe inserts
drugs.note: Cushion the heel and support the arch.

drugs.name: Corticosteroid injection
drugs.note: For stubborn pain that won't settle.

redFlags: A sudden pop with severe heel pain or being unable to put weight on the foot could mean a rupture or fracture — seek same-day care.

name: Rotator Cuff Injury
prevalence: ~2 million U.S. doctor visits each year
overview: Your rotator cuff is the group of muscles and tendons that keeps your shoulder stable and lets you raise your arm. Injuries range from inflammation and small fraying to full tears, and they're very common with age — many tears come from normal wear, not accidents. Pain often shows up when reaching overhead or lying on the sore side. Most people improve with physical therapy and don't need surgery.
symptoms: Dull ache deep in the shoulder
Pain when reaching overhead or behind the back
Pain at night, especially lying on that side
Arm weakness when lifting
Clicking or crackling with movement

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Eases pain and swelling.

drugs.name: Physical therapy
drugs.note: The mainstay — restores strength and motion.

drugs.name: Corticosteroid injection
drugs.note: Can calm pain enough to make therapy easier.

drugs.name: Rotator cuff repair
drugs.note: Surgery for full tears or pain that won't improve.

redFlags: If you can't lift your arm at all after a fall or sudden injury, the tendon may be fully torn — seek same-day care.

name: Knee Injuries (ACL & Meniscus)
prevalence: ~200,000 ACL injuries in the U.S. each year
overview: The ACL is a ligament that keeps the knee stable, and the meniscus is the cartilage cushion inside it — both are commonly injured in sports that involve pivoting, jumping, or sudden stops. A pop, swelling, and a knee that feels wobbly are classic signs. Some tears heal with physical therapy alone; others, especially ACL tears in active people, are repaired with a well-established outpatient surgery followed by months of rehab.
symptoms: A 'pop' felt or heard at the moment of injury
Rapid swelling
A knee that buckles or feels unstable
Pain along the joint line
Locking or catching when bending (meniscus)

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Eases pain and swelling after injury.

drugs.name: RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation)
drugs.note: First aid in the days after injury.

drugs.name: Physical therapy
drugs.note: Rebuilds strength and stability.

drugs.name: Arthroscopic surgery
drugs.note: Repairs or reconstructs tears through small incisions.

redFlags: A knee that looks deformed, won't bear any weight, or comes with a numb or cold foot needs emergency care — go to the ER.

name: Tendinitis
prevalence: Affects millions of Americans each year
overview: Tendinitis is irritation or inflammation of a tendon — the strong cord that attaches muscle to bone. It usually comes from repeating the same motion over and over, which is why names like tennis elbow, golfer's elbow, and jumper's knee are so familiar. The fix is rarely complicated: rest the area, ice it, ease the pain with over-the-counter medicine, and return to activity gradually.
symptoms: Dull ache where the tendon meets the bone
Tenderness when pressing on the area
Mild swelling or warmth
Pain that worsens with the repeated motion
Stiffness after rest

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: First-line relief for pain and inflammation.

drugs.name: Diclofenac gel (Voltaren)
drugs.note: Rubbed on the skin right where it hurts.

drugs.name: Rest and ice
drugs.note: Gives the tendon time to settle down.

drugs.name: Corticosteroid injection
drugs.note: For pain that doesn't improve — used sparingly.

redFlags: A sudden snap or pop followed by weakness or inability to move the joint may mean the tendon has ruptured — seek same-day care.
